questions.question: A patient with known chronic coronary disease reports chest pressure that previously occurred only after climbing two flights of stairs but now occurs while getting dressed and lasts 20 minutes. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Treat this as a changed, potentially unstable symptom pattern and arrange emergency evaluation
Schedule a routine lipid panel in 3 months
Reassure the patient because coronary disease is already known
Increase exercise to improve tolerance before reassessment
questions.explanation: Symptoms at rest, with less exertion than baseline, or of longer duration can signal acute coronary syndrome. The immediate priority is safety and emergency evaluation, not routine outpatient titration.

questions.question: Why can a rapid heart rate worsen myocardial ischemia?
choices: It increases oxygen supply and lengthens diastole
It increases myocardial oxygen demand and shortens diastolic coronary perfusion time
It eliminates wall stress
It always means a new coronary thrombus is present
questions.explanation: Tachycardia raises demand and reduces diastolic time, a major period of coronary perfusion. It can worsen supply-demand mismatch even without plaque rupture.

questions.question: Which presentation is most consistent with a chronic stable angina pattern rather than an immediate acute coronary syndrome pattern?
choices: New severe pressure at rest with diaphoresis
Predictable exertional pressure relieved by rest with no change from baseline
Pain that is longer and more frequent than last week
Chest discomfort with syncope and hypotension
questions.explanation: A reproducible exertional threshold relieved by rest can fit chronic angina, but it still merits assessment of symptom burden and prevention. New rest pain, escalation, or instability requires urgent evaluation.

questions.question: A patient with prior coronary stent says they stopped a prescribed antiplatelet because of cost. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Tell the patient to restart any leftover medication without review
Verify the procedure and intended antiplatelet plan, assess safety, and urgently coordinate access with cardiology
Assume the medication is optional because the procedure is completed
Substitute an anticoagulant without consulting the procedural plan
questions.explanation: Antiplatelet duration and selection after intervention are individualized. Medication access and prompt coordination are safety issues; antiplatelets and anticoagulants are not interchangeable.

questions.question: Before discussing a nitrate plan for angina, which medication history is especially important?
choices: Recent use of a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
A multivitamin taken last year
Topical moisturizer use
A remote antibiotic allergy only
questions.explanation: Nitrates can cause profound hypotension when combined with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors. The full medication list, blood pressure, and individualized cardiology instructions matter.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes and chronic coronary disease has new exertional dyspnea and unusual fatigue without chest pain. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Ischemia is excluded because there is no chest pain
This may be an ischemic equivalent and needs risk-based evaluation alongside alternatives
It is necessarily anxiety
It can be managed only by increasing fluid intake
questions.explanation: Ischemia can present as dyspnea, fatigue, or decreased exercise tolerance, particularly in older adults and people with diabetes. Consider cardiac and noncardiac alternatives while setting urgency by stability and risk.

questions.question: Which statement best describes secondary prevention in chronic coronary disease?
choices: It begins only after a second myocardial infarction
It combines risk-factor treatment, medication optimization when indicated, lifestyle support, rehabilitation, and follow-up
It is limited to an annual ECG
It replaces assessment of symptoms
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention actively lowers future risk through coordinated treatment of lipids, blood pressure, diabetes, tobacco use, activity, psychosocial needs, medications, and follow-up.

questions.question: A clinically stable patient with chronic coronary disease asks why every visit includes questions about exercise tolerance and symptom threshold. What is the best answer?
choices: Functional change can identify a need to reassess ischemia, heart failure, arrhythmia, medication response, or access barriers
The questions are only for insurance documentation
Symptoms never change after coronary disease is diagnosed
Exercise tolerance is unrelated to cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: Change from baseline is often the most actionable clinical information. It can indicate worsening ischemia, another cardiovascular complication, or a modifiable barrier to treatment.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly requires emergency rather than routine outpatient evaluation in a patient with known coronary disease?
choices: A stable walking routine with no symptoms
New chest discomfort with hypotension and acute dyspnea
A request for diet counseling
A medication refill question with no symptoms
questions.explanation: Hypotension and acute dyspnea with chest discomfort suggest possible hemodynamic compromise or acute coronary syndrome. Emergency assessment is required.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a closed-loop cardiology referral after a change in chronic coronary symptoms?
choices: To place an order without further responsibility
To ensure the clinical question, records, appointment, patient access, and follow-up plan are completed
To transfer all preventive care away from primary care
To avoid medication reconciliation
questions.explanation: Closed-loop coordination verifies that the referral became care. The FNP remains responsible for medication reconciliation, risk-factor management, patient education, and follow-up.
